messages.subject: Re: Stratification question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adriana, list,

If you're using a global detection function for the two species pooled=20
then you can achieve what you want in Distance using a "multiplier".=20
Look in the online help index, under "Multipliers" | "CDS and MCDS" -=20
this tells you what they are and how to use them, and also gives an=20
example very similar to yours under "Additional uses of Multipliers".

There are various other ways of combining information among species - a=20
recent paper giving some suggestions Alldredge et al (2007).  One=20
possibility might be to use the MCDS engine with species as a factor,=20
and then predict detection probability by species and use these as=20
multipliers.

For your more common species, you might also want to consider=20
stratification of the detection function by geographic area, or use of=20
the MCDS engine with area (or habitat, etc) as factors.  However, once=20
you start combining multi-species detection functions with=20
stratification/MCDS by stratum things might get a bit complicated!

Good luck with your work,

  - Len Thomas

Ref:
Alldredge, M., K.H. Pollock, T. S. & Shriner, S. 2007. Multiple-species=20
analysis of point count data: a more parsimonious modeling framework.
Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281=96290

--=20

Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: Re: Sampling in riparian strips
messages.body_plain:
Shay and list:

There is a section in the study design chapter of the introductory
distance sampling book (Buckland et al. 2001) dealing explicitly with
surveys in riparian areas.  It is section 7.8.9 on pages 300-301.

Fundamentally, you have issues of edge to area ratios being large in
habitat strips of any kind (that raises issues of uneven sampling
coverage); you also have matters of possible gradients of animal density
as you move from the edge of the river/stream to the surrounding pasture
land matrix.  The first issue is discussed in Chapter 7 of the advanced
distance sampling text (Buckland et al. 2004), and the second matter is
taken up by the thesis of Tiago Marques who has just turned in his
thesis here at St. Andrews.

Hello all distance-users,

I'm trying to get some density values from line transect data, using a
half-normal key, simple polynomial adjustment, but the density values
DISTANCE 5.0 is giving me is out by a factor of 100! (We did a manual calc

If anyone out there has had and fixed this or a similar problem, or anyone
is willing for me to send them the files so you can have a look, it would be
greatly appreciated (and you would be helping the endangered African Wild
Dog!).

My email is cla...@awdczambia.org

Claire

messages.subject: Re: FW: help! distance line transect density,
messages.body_plain:
Hi Claire, (list)

It should be relatively easy to find the source of the problem.

My guess it's that it's with the units.  By default, units of area used
to output density are the same as those you use to specify area in the
data file.  If you don't have an area field (some surveys don't -
although in general it's bad practice not to know the size of the study
area!), or want output in different units, then set this in the Data
Filter under the units tab.

If this isn't the problem, carefully check that the units of line length
and distance are what you expect (check in the data tab, the headers for
those fields).

One way to express the density calculation that distance does is simply
Dhat = n/L * 1/2w * 1/phat
where n/L is the encounter rate, w is the truncation distance and phat
is the estimated average detection probability of animals within w.  So,
if the above doesn't solve the problem, you can double check all of
these to check they are right.

To check the calculated encounter rates (i.e. number of animal seen over
line length) look right, look in the analysis details results under
Estimation Summary - Encounter rates.  You can easily calculate them by
hand to double-check.

Truncation distance used (w) is given as "Width" in the results under
Detection Fct/Global/Model fitting (or equivalent if you stratified the
detection function).

Estimated p is given under Detection Fct/Global/Parameter estimates (as
p), and also Estimation Summary - Detection probability.  Check the
estimated p seems reasonable, given the fitted detection function.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas, Distance development project coordinator
